guide.title: Rugby, Brooklyn: An 1890s Name on Utica Avenue
guide.intro: Developers chose the name Rugby in the 1890s for what is now the eastern section of East Flatbush. Building accelerated after 1892, when they acquired roughly 65 acres expecting a promised subway extension, and again once the IRT line reached Nostrand Avenue in 1912 and the area grew quickly as a residential neighborhood. Before either, in May 1900, the Brooklyn Heights Railroad extended its Reid Avenue trolley line south along Utica Avenue to reach Rugby, terminating at Utica and Church Avenues: a streetcar suburb before any subway. The Remsen name that displaced it comes from the family of Joris Remsen, an early settler and landowner, and everyday and real-estate use shifted to Remsen Village from the mid-1990s. What still carries the older name is Rugby Road and the Brooklyn Public Library's Rugby branch at 1000 Utica Avenue, which opened in 1957.

sections.heading: What survives of the name
sections.body:
Rugby is a name more than a place with edges. Sources use Rugby and Remsen Village inconsistently for the same or overlapping ground: one passage calls it the eastern section of East Flatbush, another, citing 2020 Census tabulation areas, places Rugby north of Farragut, and press coverage sometimes hyphenates the two as Rugby-Remsen Village. No source gives a single definitive line, and none is asserted here. What the research does anchor is a set of streets: Utica Avenue, Rutland Road and the East 90s, with East 98th Street described in most sourced boundary descriptions as the eastern edge.

The Rugby branch library at 1000 Utica Avenue opened in 1957. It closed in 2017 for a renovation whose budget grew from an original $1 million to $10.2 million, delayed by funding gaps, Hurricane Sandy repairs, contracting problems and the pandemic, with a mobile library trailer serving patrons in the meantime. It reopened on a Monday in July 2021 with new heating and cooling, accessibility upgrades, a garden, a mural by the artist J. Mikal Davis and sustainable materials including cork and bamboo flooring. A few blocks north, Kennedy King Playground has been city parkland since October 1957, the same year the branch opened.

By 2020 Census tabulation-area data, the Rugby area had between 30,000 and 39,999 Black residents, with the Hispanic, White and Asian populations each fewer than 5,000. In summer 2006 the New York City Department of Transportation co-named the stretch of Church Avenue from Remsen Avenue to East 98th Street as Bob Marley Boulevard, reflecting the area's large Caribbean, and particularly Jamaican, population; that co-naming is covered on the Remsen Village page.

sections.heading: Caribbean kitchens on Utica, Rutland and Church
sections.body:
The eating here is Caribbean and it clusters on three streets. On Utica Avenue, in the run of Caribbean-owned businesses between roughly 850 and 960, Tasty Caribbean sits at 856 and the Golden Krust Caribbean Bakery and Grill at 872, a few blocks south of the library. Both were graded A at their most recent city health inspections, Tasty Caribbean in October 2025 and Golden Krust in June 2026.

On Rutland Road, the commercial strip that runs out to the Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road station, Souljah at 875 is one of roughly a dozen Caribbean, Chinese and fast-food storefronts along the same stretch; it was graded A in February 2026.

On Church Avenue, inside the span co-named Bob Marley Boulevard, WB Caribbean Restaurant at 9407 and Island Flavor Jerk Cuisine at 9529 were graded A in July 2026 and April 2026. All five were located through the city's restaurant-inspection records rather than press coverage, and because no source draws a precise line between Rugby, Remsen Village and East Flatbush generally, they are grouped here on proximity to the streets the research does anchor rather than on a settled boundary.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road, on the IRT New Lots Line, sits at the meeting of Sutter Avenue, Rutland Road and East 98th Street, on the border of East Flatbush and Brownsville; sources commonly describe East 98th Street as Rugby's eastern edge. It is served by the 3 at all times except late nights, when the 4 takes over, with extra 2 and 5 service at rush hours.

The research for this page records that the IRT Nostrand Avenue Line stations, near the western border of East Flatbush and on the opposite side from Rugby's East 98th Street edge, are not a realistic access point here. That leaves the bus for the Utica Avenue side. The B46 and B46 Select Bus Service run north-south along Utica Avenue, passing the Rugby branch library at 1000 Utica Avenue, and the corridor has carried this ground since the trolley line was extended here in 1900.

faq.question: How do I get to Rugby?
faq.answer: Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road on the IRT New Lots Line, at Sutter Avenue, Rutland Road and East 98th Street, is the station at the eastern edge; it is served by the 3, with the 4 taking over late nights and extra 2 and 5 service at rush hours. For the Utica Avenue side, the B46 and B46 Select Bus Service run past the Rugby branch library.

faq.question: Is Rugby the same place as Remsen Village?
faq.answer: Sources use the two names for the same or overlapping ground. Rugby was chosen by developers in the 1890s; Remsen Village came into everyday and real-estate use from the mid-1990s, and press coverage sometimes hyphenates them as Rugby-Remsen Village. No source draws a definitive line between them.

faq.question: Where does the name Rugby come from?
faq.answer: Developers chose it in the 1890s for this section of East Flatbush. It survives on Rugby Road, on the Brooklyn Public Library's Rugby branch at 1000 Utica Avenue, which opened in 1957, and on the post office lettered Rugby Station.

faq.question: Is the Rugby branch library open?
faq.answer: Yes. It closed in 2017 for a renovation that grew from a $1 million budget to $10.2 million and was held up by funding gaps, Hurricane Sandy repairs, contracting problems and the pandemic. It reopened on a Monday in July 2021; the source that reported the reopening does not print the calendar date, so none is given here.

faq.question: What is there to eat in Rugby?
faq.answer: Caribbean cooking, on three streets. Tasty Caribbean and Golden Krust sit on Utica Avenue near the library, Souljah is on the Rutland Road strip, and WB Caribbean Restaurant and Island Flavor Jerk Cuisine are on the Church Avenue stretch co-named Bob Marley Boulevard. All five held an A grade at their most recent city health inspection.

faq.question: Are there hotels in Rugby?
faq.answer: The research for this guide found no hotel or other lodging physically inside Rugby, so none is listed rather than borrowing one from a neighbouring section of East Flatbush.

places.name: Rugby Branch, Brooklyn Public Library
places.summary: The branch opened in 1957 and is named for Rugby, the 1890s developer name for this section of East Flatbush. It closed in 2017 for renovation and reopened on a Monday in July 2021.
places.history: The renovation grew from an original $1 million budget to $10.2 million, delayed by funding gaps, Hurricane Sandy repairs, contracting problems and the pandemic; a mobile library trailer served patrons during the closure. The reopened branch has new heating and cooling, accessibility upgrades, a garden, a mural by the artist J. Mikal Davis, and cork and bamboo flooring.

places.name: Kennedy King Playground
places.summary: A 0.79-acre NYC Parks playground, operated jointly with the Department of Education, running East 93rd to East 94th Street between Lenox Road and Clarkson Avenue.
places.history: NYC Parks acquired the site on October 24, 1957, the same year the Rugby branch library opened on Utica Avenue. It falls within Community District 17; Wikipedia's account of Brooklyn Community Board 17 lists Rugby among the district's neighborhoods and gives East 98th Street as the district's eastern boundary.

places.name: Tasty Caribbean
places.summary: A Caribbean restaurant on Utica Avenue, part of a run of Caribbean-owned food businesses between roughly 850 and 960 Utica Avenue, south of the Rugby branch library. It was graded A at its most recent city health inspection, on October 20, 2025.

places.name: Golden Krust Caribbean Bakery and Grill
places.summary: A Caribbean bakery and grill, an outlet of the Golden Krust chain, a few blocks from the Rugby branch library at 1000 Utica Avenue. It was graded A at its most recent city health inspection, on June 2, 2026.

places.name: Souljah
places.summary: A Caribbean restaurant on Rutland Road, among roughly a dozen Caribbean, Chinese and fast-food storefronts along this stretch near the Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road subway station. It was graded A at its most recent city health inspection, on February 9, 2026.

places.name: WB Caribbean Restaurant
places.summary: A Caribbean restaurant on Church Avenue, inside the stretch between Remsen Avenue and East 98th Street co-named Bob Marley Boulevard in 2006. It was graded A at its most recent city health inspection, on July 22, 2026.

places.name: Island Flavor Jerk Cuisine
places.summary: A Caribbean jerk restaurant on Church Avenue, within the Remsen Avenue to East 98th Street span co-named Bob Marley Boulevard, alongside other storefronts on the same block. It was graded A at its most recent city health inspection, on April 9, 2026.

links.note: Rugby is the original name for the eastern section of East Flatbush, chosen by developers in the 1890s.
The B44 runs mostly along Nostrand Avenue through Crown Heights and Flatbush, west of the Rugby section.
